title: Want, need, must, should
title_target: Em muốn đi thăm Hạ Long.
goal: Chain verbs with no linking word at all — like "go eat" — and choose between *muốn*, *cần*, *phải*, *nên* and *định*.
bekal: stringing two to four verbs together with no connector
answering an invitation by repeating the helper verb: *Muốn chứ!*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kế hoạch cuối tuần

notes: **Verbs line up directly, with no connector at all.** *Em muốn đi thăm vịnh Hạ Long* — three verbs in a row: *muốn* (want), *đi* (go), *thăm* (visit). English has to slip in a *to* ("want to go visit"); Vietnamese slips in nothing.

**Every helper verb stands right in front of its main verb and never changes form.** *Muốn đi*, *phải đi*, *cần đi*, *nên đi*, *định đi*. There's nothing to memorize but the words themselves — no "wants", no "had to", no "to".

**Answering by repeating the helper verb is the most natural reply.** *Em cần đặt vé không?* gets *Cần chứ.*; *Anh có muốn đi không?* gets *Muốn chứ!* This follows straight from the rule in unit 2: Vietnamese has no word for "yes", so the verb itself does the answering.

**Đã at the end of a sentence means "first", not "already".** *Anh phải hỏi vợ đã* = "I have to ask my wife first". ⚠️ Don't confuse it with *đã* **before** a verb, which means "already" (unit 6). Position makes the difference — once again Vietnamese uses word order instead of changing word forms.

**Đông means "crowded" in the sense of many people** — *đông người*, *quán này đông lắm*. Its opposite is *vắng* (empty, quiet). Don't confuse it with *ồn* (noisy, unit 3): a café can be *đông* without being *ồn*, and a street can be *ồn* but *vắng*.

**Cũng được means "that works too" or "that's fine"** and it's one of the most typically Vietnamese expressions — a gentle way of saying an option is acceptable without much enthusiasm. *Đi về trong ngày cũng được.* = "a day trip would work too, I guess".

grammars.title: Eight helper verbs
body: All of them stand before the main verb, all can be negated with *không*, and all can be turned into a question with *có … không?*
after: ⚠️ **The negative of *phải* flips its meaning.** *Phải đi* = "must go", but *không phải đi* = "**don't have to** go" — not "mustn't go". To forbid, use *không được đi* (unit 12) or *đừng đi*. English has exactly the same trap (*must not* ≠ *don't have to*), so learn the three side by side: *phải đi* (must), *không phải đi* (don't have to), *không được đi* (mustn't).

*Nên* and *không nên* are the politest way to give advice — much softer than *phải*. In conversation with Vietnamese people you'll hear *nên* far more often than *phải*, because telling someone directly what to do is considered less polite.

grammars.title: Verb chains
body: Vietnamese lines verbs up like a train: one behind the other, with no couplings in between. Compare the Vietnamese and English columns — English needs *to* or *-ing* to join them; Vietnamese needs nothing.

rows: want to go buy a book
have to go buy a ticket
want to go see a friend
plan to go learn to cook

after: ⚠️ Since there are no connectors, **the order carries the meaning** — and it can't be shuffled. *Đi ăn* = go (in order) to eat; *ăn đi* = "eat up!" (a command, unit 3). The same two words, two very different meanings.

The motion verbs *đi* (go), *về* (go home), *đến* (come), *ra* (go out), *vào* (go in), *lên* (go up), *xuống* (go down) often attach to other verbs to add direction: *đi ra* (go out), *đi vào* (go in), *mang về* (take home). Much like English "take *out*", "bring *back*".

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Chơi* means "play" and is used much more widely than you'd expect: *đi chơi* (go out — not just for children), *chơi với bạn* (hang out with friends), *chơi thể thao* (play sports). If someone invites you to *đi chơi*, they're not asking you to play — they're asking you out.

Notice that almost every activity has the shape **verb + noun**, not a single word: *nấu ăn* (cook + eat), *nghe nhạc* (listen + music), *xem phim* (watch + film). So once you know the verbs, you can build new activities yourself.

blocks.title: Saying no without saying "no"
items: Turning down an invitation directly feels rude in Vietnamese culture. What people do instead: **express regret first, then give a reason** — *Tiếc quá, hôm đó em bận.* ("what a shame, I'm busy that day").
**Lần sau nhé!** ("next time, then!") is almost always added afterward, and it's not an empty promise but a sign that the relationship is still good. Refusing without it sounds cold.
